# Evolving text with GEPA

Point a reflective search at a regular expression that gets four lines in ten right, watch it read its own failures and rewrite itself, and read what the budget bought on lines the search never saw. Scoring costs nothing here, so every token goes on thinking.

**[▶ Take this lab on the Zenable Learning Hub](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=gepa-prompt-evolution&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=gepa-prompt-evolution_readme)** — fully hosted sandbox environment, progress tracking, and a full-featured lab workspace.

Eligible paid Zenable customers get an OpenRouter key automatically in their sandbox. Take the hosted version of this lab, with the key already configured, at https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=gepa-prompt-evolution&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=gepa-prompt-evolution_readme.

**Duration** 60 minutes · **Difficulty** Advanced

**Topics** `How LLMs Work` · `Verification`

**Prerequisites**

- Comfort reading Python, regular expressions and a shell prompt
- An OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini key for the reflection model, or the recorded run this rig ships

## Set up AI inference

Your sandbox has no hosted AI key. Automatic keys require an eligible paid plan and an available inference budget. Choose your own OpenRouter key, or use the local model and the lab's recorded-answer steps.

### Option A: use your own OpenRouter key

Create a key at [openrouter.ai/keys](https://openrouter.ai/keys). Then run this in the sandbox terminal, with your key in place of `sk-or-...`:

```bash
zenable-configure-inference sk-or-...
```

The command writes your key and the model settings into `~/.env` and configures every coding agent installed on the sandbox. Open a new terminal so your shell picks them up.

> [!WARNING]
> Your key goes in `~/.env`, never in the lab directory. Every attendee in the sandbox network can read the lab remote, and a key committed there is a key you've shared.

### Option B: use local Ollama (no key)

The sandbox runs [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) with a small model, `qwen3-nothink`, already downloaded and built. Point every agent at it:

```bash
zenable-configure-inference --ollama
```

Then open a new terminal. The model runs on the sandbox's CPU, so expect slower and weaker answers than a hosted model gives you. This option configures coding agents only. For steps that call Jev directly, follow the lab's recorded-answer instructions, such as adding `--fixtures` where shown. Those commands do not switch to recordings automatically.

<details>
<summary>Not on a Zenable sandbox?</summary>

For Option B, install Ollama from [ollama.com/download](https://ollama.com/download). `qwen3:1.7b` is a reasoning model, and thinking makes it very slow on a CPU, so the steps below build a copy with thinking turned off.

Download the model. Run this on its own and wait for it to finish, because the progress display takes over the terminal and swallows anything you paste behind it:

```bash
ollama pull qwen3:1.7b
```

Then build a copy of it with thinking pinned off. It reuses the weights already on disk, so there's no download and it finishes in about a second:

```bash
ollama show --modelfile qwen3:1.7b > Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|^FROM /.*|FROM qwen3:1.7b|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if and $.IsThinkSet (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|{{- if (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if $.Think -}}|{{- if false -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{ if and $.IsThinkSet (not $.Think) -}}|{{ if true -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
grep -q '{{ if true -}}' Modelfile.nothink
ollama create qwen3-nothink -f Modelfile.nothink
```

Then set the variables below in your environment, for example in a `~/.env` file that your shell loads with `set -a; . ~/.env; set +a`. Claude Code reads the `ANTHROPIC_*` variables, and agents that speak the OpenAI API, such as Codex, read `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`.

For Option A, with your OpenRouter key in place of `sk-or-...`:

```text

OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api
ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=sk-or-...
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=
ANTHROPIC_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5
ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5
```

For Option B:

## Getting started

_~8 min · Hands-on_

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Zenable-io/labs.git ~/zenable-labs 2>/dev/null \
  || git -C ~/zenable-labs pull --ff-only
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/gepa-prompt-evolution
uv sync --locked
```

The reflection model is the one thing here that needs a credential, and the rig reads it from `~/.env`, the file every new terminal exports. On a Zenable sandbox the hosted key is already there, and the rig asks OpenRouter for the sandbox's model. Anywhere else, the setup section at the top of this lab covers an OpenRouter key, and `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `GEMINI_API_KEY` work just as well.

Without a key you can still run every measurement in this lab, and read a recorded search instead of running your own. We'll point that out when we get there.

Here is the seed, which is what a person writes after reading the first few lines of a log:

```python
SEED_PATTERN = r"req_id=(\w+)"
```

Let's see how it does:

```bash
uv run python -m gepalab baseline
```

```console
pattern: req_id=(\w+)

exact-match score by split
  train        45.0%  (20 lines)
  validation   50.0%  (12 lines)
  held-out     25.0%  (8 lines)

23 lines are still wrong, the first 6:
  [2026-03-04 10:15:23] WARN  (req 8f21ad) upstream took 4.2s
    expected '8f21ad', captured '(nothing)'
  [2026-03-04 10:17:05] INFO  (req 8f21e2) cache warm, 118 keys
    expected '8f21e2', captured '(nothing)'
  trace=3b1d02 span=9c02 request-id: 8f21b0 svc=billing
    expected '8f21b0', captured '(nothing)'
  trace=3b1d55 span=9c19 request-id: 8f21f6 svc=search
    expected '8f21f6', captured '(nothing)'
  {"ts":"2026-03-04T10:15:24Z","level":"error","request_id":"8f21ae","msg":"upstream reset"}
    expected '8f21ae', captured '(nothing)'
  {"ts":"2026-03-04T10:18:11Z","level":"info","request_id":"8f2201","msg":"lease renewed"}
    expected '8f2201', captured '(nothing)'
```

It's right about the lines it was written from and silent everywhere else. Six of the forty lines carry no request id at all, and their expected answer is the empty string, so a pattern that invents one there is scored wrong like any other miss.

## Scoring is free, so the budget goes on thinking

_~12 min · Hands-on_

Here is the whole evaluator, and it's worth reading closely because it's the only thing the search knows about your problem:

```python
if outcome.correct:
    return 1.0, {"line": example.line, "feedback": "Captured the expected id."}

expected = outcome.expected or "(nothing, this line has no request id)"
captured = outcome.captured or "(nothing)"
return 0.0, {
    "line": example.line,
    "expected": expected,
    "captured": captured,
    "feedback": f"Expected {expected} but captured {captured}.",
}
```

A score, and a sentence. The score drives selection; the sentence is what the reflection model reads.

A pattern that fails to compile is a normal move in this search, so it scores zero and hands back the error rather than raising:

```python
except PatternError as error:
    return 0.0, {
        "line": example.line,
        "expected": example.request_id,
        "feedback": f"The pattern does not compile: {error}",
    }
```

You can score any pattern you like against the same splits. Let's try the fix most people reach for first, which is to accept the other field names:

```bash
uv run python -m gepalab score '(?:req_id|request_id|requestId|request-id|rid)\s*[:=]\s*(?P<id>[A-Za-z0-9_-]+)' --misses 3
```

```console
pattern: (?:req_id|request_id|requestId|request-id|rid)\s*[:=]\s*(?P<id>[A-Za-z0-9_-]+)

exact-match score by split
  train        60.0%  (20 lines)
  validation   83.3%  (12 lines)
  held-out     50.0%  (8 lines)

14 lines are still wrong, the first 3:
  [2026-03-04 10:15:23] WARN  (req 8f21ad) upstream took 4.2s
    expected '8f21ad', captured '(nothing)'
  [2026-03-04 10:17:05] INFO  (req 8f21e2) cache warm, 118 keys
    expected '8f21e2', captured '(nothing)'
  {"ts":"2026-03-04T10:15:24Z","level":"error","request_id":"8f21ae","msg":"upstream reset"}
    expected '8f21ae', captured '(nothing)'
```

Better on every split, and fourteen lines still wrong. The `(req 8f21ad)` form has no separator at all, and the JSON lines quote the field name, so a pattern expecting a colon straight after `request_id` walks past them.

That is the loop we are about to hand over: read what missed, work out what the pattern assumed, write a version that assumes less.

Question: our evaluator returns the line, the expected value and the captured value on every failure. What would the search lose if it returned only the score?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The ability to tell two failures apart.

"Scored zero" is the same signal whether the pattern captured nothing, captured a neighbouring `session_id`, dragged a quote along, or failed to compile. Each of those calls for a different next edit, and a number can't say which one happened.

The reflection model only ever sees your problem through these strings. A sparse evaluator makes an expensive model guess at what a cheap sentence could have told it.

</details>

## Letting the search rewrite it

_~15 min · Hands-on_

One command. Three hundred evaluations, eight scored lines put in front of the reflection model each round:

```bash
uv run python -m gepalab evolve --budget 300 --reflect-on 8
```

GEPA prints a line per iteration, saying which candidate it selected, what it proposed, and whether the proposal beat what it already had.

```console
reflecting with bedrock/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5, budget 300 evaluations
...
Iteration 0: Base program full valset score: 0.5 over 12 / 12 examples
Iteration 1: Selected program 0 score: 0.5
Iteration 1: Proposed new text for current_candidate:
Iteration 1: New subsample score 3.0 is not better than old score 4.0, skipping
Iteration 2: Selected program 0 score: 0.5
Iteration 2: Proposed new text for current_candidate: (?:(?:req_id|rid|request-id)\s*[:=]\s*["']?|"(?:request_id|requestId)"\s*:\s*"|(?:INFO|WARN|ERROR|DEBUG|TRACE)\s+\[)(?P<id>[\w-]+)
Iteration 3: Selected program 1 score: 0.9166666666666666
Iteration 3: Proposed new text for current_candidate: (?:(?:req_id|rid|request-id)\s*[:=]\s*["']?|"(?:request_id|requestId)"\s*:\s*"|(?:INFO|WARN|ERROR|DEBUG|TRACE)\s+\(req\s+|(?:INFO|WARN|ERROR|DEBUG|TRACE)\s+\[)(?P<id>[\w-]+)
Iteration 4: Selected program 2 score: 1.0
...
Iteration 19: Reflective mutation did not propose a new candidate

seed
  train        45.0%  (20 lines)
  validation   50.0%  (12 lines)
  held-out     25.0%  (8 lines)

best candidate
  train       100.0%  (20 lines)
  validation  100.0%  (12 lines)
  held-out    100.0%  (8 lines)

best candidate:
  (?:(?:req_id|rid|request-id)\s*[:=]\s*["']?|"(?:request_id|requestId)"\s*:\s*"|(?:INFO|WARN|ERROR|DEBUG|TRACE)\s+\(req\s+|(?:INFO|WARN|ERROR|DEBUG|TRACE)\s+\[)(?P<id>[\w-]+)
```

Iteration 1 proposed nothing usable, which happens: that reflection ran out of room mid-sentence, and what came back couldn't compile.

Iteration 2 read eight scored lines and came back with the field names, the quoted JSON key and the bracket form in one pattern, and that took validation from 50% to 91.7%.

Iteration 3 added the one shape still missing, `(req 8f21ad)`, and hit 100%. Everything after that is the search trying and failing to beat itself.

Without a key, nothing above runs, so the rig ships the run that produced everything above. Read it with:

```bash
uv run python -m gepalab show
```

```console
run regex, reflected with bedrock/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5
300 evaluations, 3 candidates kept

seed
  train        45.0%  (20 lines)
  validation   50.0%  (12 lines)
  held-out     25.0%  (8 lines)

best candidate
  train       100.0%  (20 lines)
  validation  100.0%  (12 lines)
  held-out    100.0%  (8 lines)

seed:
  req_id=(\w+)

best candidate:
  (?:(?:req_id|rid|request-id)\s*[:=]\s*["']?|"(?:request_id|requestId)"\s*:\s*"|(?:INFO|WARN|ERROR|DEBUG|TRACE)\s+\(req\s+|(?:INFO|WARN|ERROR|DEBUG|TRACE)\s+\[)(?P<id>[\w-]+)
```

The reflection model is named in that first line because it's the one thing about a run that the run cannot tell you afterwards. Ours went through Bedrock; a run against `openai/gpt-5.1` reaches a different pattern, and that difference is the reflection model doing its job.

## What the budget bought, and what it didn't

_~8 min · Hands-on_

Three splits, three numbers, and only one of them is evidence.

Validation is what the search optimised against: it kept whichever candidate scored best there, so a good validation number is partly a report on its own taste. Train is what it read while proposing. Held-out is the eight lines nothing in the run ever touched.

That's the number worth having, and it moved as far as the other two. The pattern learned the shapes rather than the twelve lines it was scored on.

A word on how far that licenses you to trust it. Forty lines is a fixture, not a log. The honest use of this rig is to point the same evaluator at a thousand of your own lines, and the honest reading of a 100% on eight held-out lines is that nothing has contradicted the pattern yet.

Now the budget. Look back at the run and find where the winner appeared:

```bash
uv run python -m gepalab show --lineage
```

```console
what the search kept, in the order it found them:
  0. [50.0%] req_id=(\w+)
  1. [91.7%] (?:(?:req_id|rid|request-id)\s*[:=]\s*["']?|"(?:request_id|requestId)"\s*:\s*"|(?:INFO|WARN|ERROR|DEBUG|TRACE)\s+\[)(?P<id>[\w-]+)
  2. [100.0%] (?:(?:req_id|rid|request-id)\s*[:=]\s*["']?|"(?:request_id|requestId)"\s*:\s*"|(?:INFO|WARN|ERROR|DEBUG|TRACE)\s+\(req\s+|(?:INFO|WARN|ERROR|DEBUG|TRACE)\s+\[)(?P<id>[\w-]+)
```

Three candidates over three hundred evaluations, and the winner is the one found at iteration 3. Everything after that was the search failing to beat itself.

So `--budget` is a ceiling rather than a target. Most of that budget bought nothing here, and on a task where scoring costs a model call rather than a microsecond, that's most of the bill.

The other knob is how much of the problem the reflection model sees at once:

```python
reflection=ReflectionConfig(
    reflection_lm=model,
    reflection_minibatch_size=args.reflect_on,
```

GEPA defaults that to three. Three failures out of forty is a keyhole, and a proposal written through it comes back tuned to whichever lines happened to be in front of it. This rig asks for eight, which is why `--reflect-on` is a flag you can turn rather than a number buried in the call.

Question: this whole run cost about a dime, because scoring a regex is free. What changes about every decision above when the thing being scored is a model call?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The budget stops being a ceiling and starts being the bill. Three hundred evaluations of a program that calls a model is three hundred model calls per run, and a validation set of twelve is twelve of them for every candidate kept.

That is why the split sizes and the stopping point matter more there than here, and why an optimiser that picks demonstrations rather than rewriting instructions is often the cheaper first move. The [DSPy lab](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=dspy-programs&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=gepa-prompt-evolution_readme) runs exactly that trade on a model small enough to keep on your own machine.

</details>
